intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that early-onset dystonia and/or spastic paraplegia (DYTSPG) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ATP5MC3 gene (602736) on chromosome 2q31.1.

checks.claim: Early-onset dystonia and/or spastic paraplegia (DYTSPG) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the ATP5MC3 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: ATP5MC3 has already been suggested as a candidate gene for autosomal-dominant phenotypes. In the independent pedigree, c.318C>G was detected among 18 individuals with variable dystonia-spasticity presentations
checks.explanation: Paper links heterozygous (de novo) ATP5MC3 variants to dystonia/spasticity but does not name the DYTSPG entity.

checks.claim: The ATP5MC3 gene is located on chromosome 2q31.1.
checks.evidence_quote: Three patients had de novo heterozygous missense variants in ATP5F1A, whereas another 3 were heterozygous for ATP5MC3 de novo missense changes.
checks.explanation: Gene discussed; chromosomal location not stated in paper but is standard nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Early-onset dystonia and/or spastic paraplegia (DYTSPG) is an autosomal dominant neurologic disorder with variable presentation. Affected individuals may have childhood-onset, progressive generalized dystonia or milder focal dystonia, including within a single family. Some patients also have developmental delay and pyramidal signs. Patient fibroblasts show reduced activity of mitochondrial complex V (ATP synthase).

checks.evidence_quote: The autosomal dominant pedigree included 40 individuals, of which 18 were affected with either childhood-onset, progressive generalized dystonia or adult-onset, gradually progressive spastic paraplegia.
checks.explanation: The paper describes autosomal dominant inheritance of the dystonia/spastic paraplegia phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Gilbert et al. (2009) reported a large multigenerational Ohio kindred with autosomal dominant hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) and dystonia. Spasticity and weakness began between the first year and the sixth decade of life, and dystonia between the first and third decades. Generalized dystonia was described in 1 affected child. The family had no ataxia and no apparent cognitive involvement. Neuroimaging and peripheral neurophysiology were normal.

paragraphs.text: Neilson et al. (2022) reported a family (Family-1) with an autosomal dominant pedigree of 40 individuals. Eighteen were affected with either childhood-onset, progressive generalized dystonia or adult-onset, gradually progressive spastic paraplegia with progressive leg weakness. Some family members had less severe, later-onset focal limb and neck dystonia and spasmodic dysphonia, which the authors suggested might be related to trauma or overuse. The authors stated that dystonia could generalize when it began in childhood, showed incomplete penetrance, and responded to pallidal deep brain stimulation. The spastic paraplegia began in adulthood (after age 20 years), progressed gradually, and was not accompanied by other neurologic problems. In the proband, dystonia began in one upper limb at age 2 years and generalized to the trunk and all limbs, leading to loss of ambulation. Brain MRI and peripheral nerve physiology were normal. Blood lactate and pyruvate were normal in the 2 individuals tested.

paragraphs.text: Neilson et al. (2022) also reported a second, unrelated patient (Family-2). He was a right-handed boy born to healthy, unrelated parents of European descent with no family history of dystonia or related movement disorders. He first presented at age 11 years with a 4-year history of gradually worsening upper limb dystonia. Brain MRI showed nonspecific, mild, bilateral frontoparietal white-matter changes without other abnormalities.

paragraphs.text: Zech et al. (2022) reported 3 unrelated patients with dystonia and/or spasticity. Patient 8 was the boy previously reported by Neilson et al. (2022); at 12 years of age he had isolated upper-limb dystonia. Patient 9 was a 15-year-old girl with a history of milestone delay, pyramidal signs, and generalized dystonia with prominent upper-body involvement. Patient 10 was a 6-year-old French boy with delayed psychomotor development, lower-extremity spasticity, and elevated blood lactate. Zech et al. (2022) combined these patients with the multigenerational family of Neilson et al. (2022). Across these individuals, dystonia was present in 12 of 18, spasticity or pyramidal signs in 17 of 18, and developmental delay or intellectual disability in 2 of 18.

paragraphs.text: Neilson et al. (2022) studied fibroblasts from the Family-1 proband, who had dystonia, and his affected father, who had HSP. Activities of complexes I through IV were normal, but complex V activity was reduced by 20%. Cellular ATP was reduced by 20 to 32% and oxygen consumption by 21 to 25%. Because oxygen consumption and ATP fell in proportion, the results did not support uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation.

paragraphs.text: Gilbert et al. (2009) performed single and multipoint linkage analysis with microsatellite and SNP array genotyping in a large multigenerational Ohio kindred with HSP and dystonia. They mapped the disease locus to chromosome 2q24-q31, between markers rs1424937 and rs1559510. The region lies proximal to SPG13 and contained no known HSP or dystonia genes. In a secondary analysis looking for candidate regions that segregated with the dystonia phenotype, they found 2 regions with parametric lod scores above 2.0.

paragraphs.text: Neilson et al. (2022) noted that linkage analysis in their large family (Family-1) had previously mapped the disorder to chromosome 2q24-q31. Whole-exome sequencing restricted to this region identified a heterozygous missense mutation in the ATP5MC3 gene (c.318C-G; N106K) as the only shared novel coding variant. Sanger sequencing showed that only affected family members carried the variant. In a second, unrelated patient (Family-2), trio whole-exome sequencing identified the same N106K mutation in the heterozygous state, occurring de novo. Fibroblasts from Family-1 patients showed reduced complex V activity, and Drosophila carrying the equivalent mutation had reduced mobility and reduced complex V activity. Screening of ATP5MC1, ATP5MC2, and ATP5MC3 in 384 patients with dystonia (n = 362) or HSP (n = 22) found no deleterious variants.

paragraphs.text: Neilson et al. (2022) noted that 2 paralogs, ATP5MC1 and ATP5MC2, also encode subunit c, so haploinsufficiency of ATP5MC3 would be unlikely to explain the severe phenotypes. They hypothesized that the mutant protein interferes with the F1-F0 interaction at a conserved loop. They suggested that relative expression of the mutant gene in different tissues may influence whether dystonia or spastic paraplegia develops.

paragraphs.text: Zech et al. (2022) suggested that dominant-negative effects could underlie the disease caused by ATP5MC3 mutations. This was supported by mild to moderate defects in ATPase assembly and/or enzyme activity in patient cell lines. paragraphs.text: In affected members of a large family (Family-1) with autosomal dominant dystonia and/or spastic paraplegia, Neilson et al. (2022) identified a heterozygous c.318C-G transversion (NM_001689.4) in the ATP5MC3 gene, resulting in an asn106-to-lys (N106K) substitution. The family had 18 affected members, with childhood-onset generalized dystonia, adult-onset spastic paraplegia, or milder focal dystonia. The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing restricted to the linked region on chromosome 2q24-q31, and Sanger sequencing showed that only affected individuals carried it. Fibroblasts from 2 affected family members showed a 20% reduction in complex V activity, with reduced cellular ATP and oxygen consumption. Drosophila carrying the equivalent mutation showed reduced mobility and reduced complex V activity. In an unrelated boy of European descent (Family-2) with upper limb dystonia beginning at age 7 years, Neilson et al. (2022) identified the same N106K mutation in the heterozygous state by trio whole-exome sequencing; it had occurred de novo.

paragraphs.text: In a 6-year-old French boy (patient 10) with delayed psychomotor development, lower-extremity spasticity, and elevated blood lactate, Zech et al. (2022) identified a de novo heterozygous c.236G-T transversion in the ATP5MC3 gene, resulting in a gly79-to-val (G79V) substitution. The variant affected a strictly conserved residue and was absent from gnomAD. Patient fibroblasts showed deficient ATPase activity and a moderate decrease in assembled ATPase on blue native PAGE. The ATPase deficit was significantly greater than that caused by the N106K mutation.
